title: A Human-AI Theorem Connecting Spontaneous and Field-Induced Mechanisms of Collective Behavior in One Dimension
abstract: Can an artificial intelligence (AI) generate a scientific hypothesis outside a human collaborator's active hypothesis space (AHS), and can human-AI research be organized to make such breakthroughs more likely? We document such a case while proving a theorem that connects two basic organizing mechanisms of statistical physics: collective behavior arising in zero field from competing interactions and that induced or controlled by an external field. A zero-field $O(n)$-vector open chain with arbitrary inhomogeneous nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor interaction functions $U_i(S_i\cdot{S}_{i+1})$ and $V_i(S_i\cdot{S}_{i+2})$ is microscopically, via a temperature-independent mapping at the Hamiltonian level, equivalent to a simpler $O(n)$ open chain with nearest-neighbor interaction $V_i( σ_i\cdot σ_{i+1})$ and axial single-spin potential $U_i(σ_i^z)$ for every integer $n\ge1$ and every system size $L\ge1$. The homogeneous linear specialization maps the foundational frustrated $J_1$-$J_2$ model onto the canonical $J$-$h$ field model---with $n=1,2,3$ being the Ising, XY, and Heisenberg classical spin models, respectively. An analogous theorem holds when the continuous $O(n)$ spins are replaced by the $q$-state Potts spins with the standard Potts interaction, implying a closed-form exact solution of the $J_1$-$J_2$ Potts open chain for every $q\ge2$ and every $L\ge1$. The emergence of the theorems from sustained human-AI collaboration suggests that involving AI throughout a systematic research program may incubate autonomous scientific breakthroughs.
summary: This paper proves a general theorem connecting two distinct ways collective behavior can emerge in 1D spin chains: spontaneously via competing interactions, and externally via a field. It establishes an exact, Hamiltonian-level mapping between complex range-two interactions and simpler range-one interactions for both continuous and discrete spin systems. The work also frames this discovery within a novel model of human-AI scientific collaboration.
main_problem: The paper aims to connect two fundamental mechanisms of collective behavior in statistical physics: those arising spontaneously from competing interactions (zero field) and those controlled by an external field.
main_result: A theorem is proven establishing a microscopic, temperature-independent mapping between a range-two Hamiltonian (with nearest and next-nearest neighbor interactions) and a simpler range-one Hamiltonian (with nearest-neighbor and single-spin potential).
method: The mapping is established using exact mathematical techniques, including a recursive Householder moving frame construction for continuous spins and kinematic identities for the Potts model.
model_or_system: The models are one-dimensional open chains of classical spins, including $O(n)$-vector spins (Ising, XY, Heisenberg) and the $q$-state Potts model. The Hamiltonians involve arbitrary inhomogeneous nearest-neighbor and next-nearest-neighbor interactions.
key_observables: The partition function ($Z$) and the equivalence between the two Hamiltonian forms.
important_parameters: The dimensionality $n$ (for $O(n)$ spins), the number of states $q$ (for Potts spins), and the system size $L$.
main_assumptions: The mapping is shown to hold for arbitrary inhomogeneous interactions and finite system sizes, overcoming previous limitations in the thermodynamic limit.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the research trajectory, showing the progression from an initial Active Hypothesis Space (AHS) to a broader space driven by Human-AI collaboration.
paper_structure: The paper develops the theoretical framework by first defining the two Hamiltonian forms, then proving the exact mapping for both continuous $O(n)$ spins and discrete $q$-state Potts spins, and finally framing the discovery process within a human-AI collaboration model.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical mapping provides a powerful tool for solving complex 1D lattice models, which is foundational knowledge for understanding quantum many-body systems and their classical limits.
